questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Real values destroyed by a sentinel recode
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a sentinel code can destroy real readings
questions.stem: Explain to a club member why recoding missing hive weights as a special number can quietly destroy real measurements.

answer.exemplar: A sentinel code such as -999 is meant to mark absent entries, but the same value may occur as a genuine reading, and the values are then mixed with real measurements. Once merged, no later summary can tell which readings were observed, so an outlier analysis may treat real extremes as recording errors and drop them.

questions.explanation: A sentinel works only if its value cannot occur naturally, and readers cannot recover the distinction after merging. Using a clearly impossible value and keeping a separate missingness flag preserves the information.
questions.hint: A code must be impossible in real data.

questions.stem: During an export my 20 measured hive weights were converted to text, and 5 cells held a dash that was then read as zero. What is the mean of the 15 remaining real values if they total 96?
questions.explanation: The 96 units belong to the 15 real measurements, so the mean of the true values is 96 over 15, which is 6.4. Averaging over all 20 rows gives 4.8 and understates every hive, because dashes still divide.
questions.hint: Divide the total by the count of real values only.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Mean biased by text cells coerced to zero
questions.learningObjective: Explain why text placeholders distort an average
questions.stem: Explain to a new member why averaging hive weights that include text cells read as zero gives a misleading result.

answer.exemplar: When some cells arrive as text and are converted to zero, those cells enter the mean as real measurements of nothing, which pulls the average down by an amount that depends on how many were converted rather than on any change in the colonies. The bias grows with the number of converted cells, so the same colony set can produce different averages depending only on the export settings.

questions.explanation: Zero is a legitimate weight, so converted cells are indistinguishable from genuine zeros and silently drag the average down. The bias depends on how many cells were converted, which makes it easy to miss in a table.
questions.hint: Zero looks like data to a spreadsheet.

answer.exemplar: An export that stops partway through the season omits every later entry, so the file supports statements about the period it covers and nothing beyond it. questions.topic: Mean biased by text cells coerced to zero
questions.learningObjective: Explain why converting gaps to zero lowers a mean
questions.stem: Explain to a new keeper why my season mean falls once some harvest cells are converted to zero.

answer.exemplar: Zero is an ordinary weight that the averaging step includes, so every cell converted from a blank contributes nothing to the total while still enlarging the divisor. The mean therefore falls by an amount that depends on how many gaps were converted, and the same colonies produce different means depending only on the export settings.

questions.explanation: The bias comes from gaps entering the arithmetic as measurements of nothing. The size of the effect depends on the number of conversions, so the error is invisible unless the count of genuine readings is reported alongside the mean.
questions.hint: Zero is a number, so it joins the average.

answer.exemplar: The rate quantifies how much of the variable was never observed, which sets a ceiling on the strength of any summary drawn from it. questions.explanation: Missingness limits coverage and may hide a pattern, and the rate is the cheapest honest description of that limit. Randomness reduces but does not remove the concern, since it is a belief, not a tested fact.
questions.hint: Coverage is the basic thing to report.

questions.stem: Why can a consent sheet be formally complete and still fail to produce a valid agreement?

options.text: Because a valid agreement requires the sheet to be printed on club letterhead
options.misconception: Believing stationery carries legal weight in consent

options.text: It may list every clause yet be read too fast for anyone to understand what they accepted
Because the sheet must be witnessed by two other club members
options.misconception: Believing witness counts are required for an agreement to hold

options.text: Because the sheet has to be filed with the county group within seven days
options.misconception: Believing a filing deadline determines whether consent is valid

questions.explanation: Validity depends on understanding and freedom at the moment of agreement, which a full clause list does not deliver if nobody checked comprehension. Letterhead, witnesses and filing dates are beside the point.
questions.hint: Completeness is not comprehension.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Rate of missingness on one variable
questions.learningObjective: Compute how many rows a summary covers
questions.stem: My logbook has 240 rows and the weight column is blank in 30 of them. If I report the mean over rows that carry a weight, how many rows does that mean rest on?

options.text: A complete weight summary for the season, since only one column is affected
options.misconception: Believing one incomplete column cannot affect a season summary

options.text: 240 rows, with the blank cells treated as zero weights
options.misconception: Believing blanks can be counted as zero readings without any note

options.text: 210 rows, once the 30 blank rows are set aside
No weight summary at all, since 30 missing readings make the variable unusable
options.misconception: Believing twelve missing rows disqualify a usable variable

questions.explanation: 240 minus 30 leaves 210 rows with a recorded weight, and that is the number of observations behind the mean. Reporting the count alongside the figure tells a reader how much of the season the summary covers.
questions.hint: Subtract the blank rows from the total.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Real values destroyed by a sentinel recode
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a sentinel code destroys real readings
questions.stem: Explain to a new keeper why storing missing weights as the number -999 can destroy real readings.

answer.exemplar: The marker only works if the value cannot occur naturally, and hive readings can reach any number a scale reports, including a fault value such as -999. Once blanks and genuine readings share one code, no later analysis can tell them apart, so an outlier rule may discard a real reading or a summary may count a missing entry as a measurement.

questions.explanation: The sentinel and the real reading become indistinguishable the moment they are stored the same way, so the loss is silent and permanent. A flag kept beside an empty cell, or a marker no reading can take, avoids it.
questions.hint: The marker must be a value data cannot take.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Mean biased by text cells coerced to zero
questions.learningObjective: Compute a mean over genuine readings only
questions.stem: In my harvest log, 8 of 90 weight cells were text entries read as zero, and the 82 real values total 287. What is the mean of the real values?
questions.explanation: The 287 units belong to the 82 genuine readings, so their mean is 287 over 82, exactly 3.5. Including the eight converted cells as zeros gives 3.19 and describes a harvest that never happened.
questions.hint: Divide the total by the count of genuine readings.
